turns.text: Can you tell me about the moment you first learned you would be sent down to the countryside? What did you see, hear, or feel in that instant?

I was standing in our cramped kitchen, the smell of cabbage and coal dust thick in the air, when my father came home with the assignment notice. He didn’t say anything at first—just handed me the paper, his mouth pressed into a line. I could hear my youngest sister in the next room, humming as she tried to finish her homework. The paper felt heavier than it should. I remember the red stamp, the official words, but what I really remember is the quiet that fell in the house. My mother’s hands stopped moving. I could hear my own heartbeat. Outside, someone was shouting slogans, but in that moment, all the noise seemed far away. My chest tightened, not from surprise, but from the certainty that everything was about to change, and I had no say in it. I felt cold, even though it was summer.

I can almost feel that hush you described, and the way the ordinary details—like your sister humming—suddenly took on new weight. When you looked at your parents in that moment, did you sense what they were feeling, or notice anything in how they acted or spoke to you afterward?

My father kept his eyes on the floor, shifting his weight from foot to foot like he wanted to disappear. He was never a talkative man, but that night he was even quieter, eating his rice with tiny bites, not looking up. My mother tried to act normal, asking if I wanted more soup, but her voice was too bright and her hands trembled when she ladled it. Later, when she thought I was asleep, I heard her crying softly in the next room. The next morning, my parents both left for work earlier than usual, and my mother didn’t say goodbye. It was as if they didn’t know how to face me, or maybe they were afraid of saying the wrong thing. For the first time, I realized they were powerless too.

It’s striking, how your parents’ fear and powerlessness seeped into those small gestures—like your mother’s trembling hands and your father’s silence. After that night, did you find yourself looking at them differently, or did it change how you felt about the family expectations you carried as the eldest?

I started noticing things I hadn’t before—the lines on my father’s face, the way he seemed smaller when he walked through the door. I used to think of my parents as unshakeable, but after that night, I saw how much they were just trying to hold things together. I felt heavier, like their hopes and disappointments were suddenly loaded onto my back. As the eldest, I’d always been told to set a good example, but now it felt more like I was being sent out as a shield, to take the first blow so the others might be spared. At the same time, I felt angry, though I tried not to show it. I kept wondering if they could have fought harder for me, even though I knew deep down they had no choice.

That sense of being both a protector and a sacrifice, while also feeling anger at your parents’ helplessness, sounds like a heavy burden for someone so young. When the day finally came for you to leave Shanghai, what did you take with you—physically and emotionally—as you said goodbye to your home and your family?

I packed a small canvas bag with two sets of clothes, a tin of biscuits my mother pressed into my hand, and a notebook with a soft blue cover. My mother tucked a red scarf into the bottom of my bag, something of hers for luck, though she didn’t say it out loud. I tried not to look at my sisters too much; the youngest clung to my skirt and wouldn’t let go until my father pried her away. The apartment smelled like damp concrete and boiled rice. My mother stood in the doorway, face blotchy from crying, but she kept her back straight. My father walked me to the bus stop but said nothing, just squeezed my shoulder before turning away. I felt like I was watching myself from the outside, numb and hollow, trying to memorize the sound of the street vendors and the way the city looked in the morning light. I carried a knot in my stomach, a mix of dread and guilt, wondering if I would ever see any of it again.

The way you describe trying to memorize the city—the sounds, the light—makes me think about how you must have been trying to hold onto pieces of home even as you left. After you boarded the bus and Shanghai faded from view, do you remember what went through your mind, or any moment during that journey north that stands out most sharply in your memory?

I sat by the window, pressed against the glass, watching the city blur into gray factories and then endless fields. At first I tried to count the smokestacks, but I lost track. There was a boy across the aisle, about my age, clutching a pillow to his chest and staring straight ahead. The bus rattled and groaned, and the farther we got, the quieter everyone became. At one point, we stopped at a tiny station in the middle of nowhere, and I stepped outside for a moment. The air was sharper, colder, and I remember looking up at a sky that seemed much bigger than the one over Shanghai. I felt suddenly very small, as if I’d been dropped into someone else’s life. That was the first time I realized I couldn’t just go back whenever I wanted. The road behind us was already gone.

That feeling of the sky being bigger and the road behind you disappearing—did it make you feel more determined to survive, or did it just make the loneliness sharper? In those first days after arriving, did the vastness of the place make you think differently about the promises and slogans you’d heard back in Shanghai?

The loneliness was like a stone in my chest, heavier than anything I’d felt before. At first, the vastness just made me feel lost—like I could vanish and no one would notice. The fields seemed to stretch forever, and the wind never stopped. I remembered the slogans painted on walls back home, all about hope and building a new life, but out there, those words felt empty. My hands ached from work I’d never done before, and my shoes filled with mud. I started to wonder if the people who wrote those promises had ever set foot in a place like this. I didn’t feel determined, not yet. Mostly I was just trying to get through each day without breaking down.

Hearing how the slogans felt hollow against the reality of aching hands and endless fields makes me think about the gap between official words and lived experience. Was there a particular task or moment during those first weeks—maybe something with the mud or the wind—that made you realize just how different life would be from what you’d been told to expect?

The first time I was sent to work in the paddies, I thought I understood hard labor, but I didn’t. The mud sucked at my feet so deeply I lost a shoe within the first hour. The water was icy, numbing my ankles and shins until I couldn’t feel where my legs ended. My hands blistered from gripping the stalks, and the wind cut through my jacket, carrying the smell of wet earth and something sour I couldn’t name. We worked in lines, but the field was so wide that the person at the other end looked like a speck. I remember glancing up and seeing nothing but gray sky and brown water, no buildings, no voices except the occasional shout from a team leader. That was when it hit me—no one cared if I was tired or scared or lost. The slogans in Shanghai never mentioned the cold, or the way your body could ache in places you didn’t know existed. That day, I stopped believing anyone would save me.

The image of you losing your shoe in the sucking mud and feeling invisible in that endless field is so vivid—it’s such a stark contrast to the crowded city you left behind. Did you find any way to comfort yourself after those first brutal days, or did you just try to shut down your feelings to get through it?
